beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new, just a header

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Output looking fine doesn't prove safety, so you need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new, a reading list I won't open

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: There is a named list of agent risks, and I want to see whether I've covered them.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: Start by listing what I'd check before exposing the system to anyone.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: nothing new, I use tool calls every day. The 'text crossing a boundary' framing is tidy, though.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: A rhetorical hook. Honestly, no, I wouldn't bet on mine.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: nothing new, I know classical security

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: The attack surface is the instructions the agent reads, so any document it ingests can steer it. I hadn't thought about that for our org-wide setups.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five named mitigations, a useful vocabulary. Most I do already without naming them.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.
beats.got: You may record 'I can't tell' as a result. It reads a bit like ceremony to me.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: There's a real tradeoff, and I normally push for more access, not less.

beats.trigger: Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it.
beats.got: Ask whether each connection is needed before wiring it in. That's the opposite of how I built the sales setup.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new, a motivational wrap-up

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: We'll package a security check as a skill so it can be rerun. I know skills, and this is something I could roll out to others.

beats.trigger: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The raw policy run sorts rules into what the files can verify and what needs a human.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell the agent what matters here in my own words, and it shapes the package around that instead of a template.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent interviews me and builds a two-lens skill, one for policy and one for agent risk.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: When the questions get long, I can hand the choice back to the agent. That shortcut is handy.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: Install the skill and check it's there. Plumbing, nothing new.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The skill is source material plus judgment, and it doesn't replace our existing controls.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: This exercise runs the loop once on my own system, and a clean result isn't the goal.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new, check that the skill shows up

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit flagged things I assumed were fine and marked others 'can't tell'. Some of my 'it's fine' was only a feeling.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The ranked risk report shows where my system is exposed, and the uncomfortable parts are the useful ones.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: Apply one mitigation, re-run, and write down what's left. I wanted to keep fixing, but the exercise says stop.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: When stuck, take the specific question to legal or security instead of prompting more.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One mitigation doesn't make production. All of my org-wide setups are prototypes by this standard.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The skill is reusable for the next agent, and the report holds the evidence.

beats.trigger: Two things travel: the reusable check, and the root instructions file's rules for the risk you found.
beats.got: The agent writes what we learned into the root instructions file, so future sessions inherit the lesson.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills are shareable methods, not services, and ownership is a separate question. That's the maintenance issue I'd skipped for my sales setup.

beats.trigger: Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.
beats.got: nothing new, a summary of what I just did

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework with a nudge. I'd probably skip it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases where nobody checked the output. I'm curious about those.

take_homes: Agents can be steered by plain text in anything they read, so before connecting a source I should ask whether the agent needs it at all.
'I can't tell' is a legitimate audit result, and my 'it looks fine' was often just a feeling. The packaged audit skill catches that.
A skill I can rerun against each new agent beats re-prompting. One mitigation plus a written-down residual is a prototype, not production.

monday.move: Run the agent-audit skill against the sales-team setup I built, pick the top-ranked risk, and cut its access (scope down or add a gate).
monday.who: me, then show the report to whoever would own maintenance, probably someone in security or IT
monday.stop_condition: One mitigation applied and the residual written in the report. I don't rebuild anything else.
monday.blocker: I still haven't checked who maintains the sales setup, and the audit doesn't answer that.

misconception.why: The audit flagged things I thought were fine and left things as 'can't tell', so a good-looking setup still had gaps I hadn't checked. I'd still skip checks on routine work, but not on anything org-wide.

one_line: first half is slow if you run agents already, but the audit found stuff i'd skipped and the 'don't open the door' bit changed how i'd wire up the sales setup.
